Coverage of PySAL giddy

Source: vignettes/articles/giddy-coverage.Rmd
giddy-coverage.Rmd

The methods in griddy come from the spatial distribution dynamics literature, most directly the spatial Markov chain of Rey (2001) and the homogeneity tests studied by Rey, Kang, and Wolf (2016). Their reference implementation is PySAL giddy. griddy implements the same methods in R, for long sf panels with tidy outputs.

griddy is not a port of giddy. It uses giddy as a validation oracle rather than as a specification. Static fixtures from giddy 2.3.9 check the classic and spatial Markov counts and probabilities, sojourn and first-passage times, the mobility indices, and the Pearson and likelihood-ratio homogeneity statistics. Some giddy features take only a few lines of griddy, sfdep, dplyr, or base R, and are documented here as recipes rather than added as functions.

This article maps every public entry of giddy 2.3.9 onto griddy.

How to read the table

Each entry falls into one of four categories:

  • Implemented: a griddy function covers it.
  • Composition: there is no dedicated function, but a short recipe built from griddy, sfdep, dplyr, or base R produces the same result. The longer recipes are worked through below, with checks against giddy 2.3.9 output.
  • Planned: deliberately deferred to a later release.
  • Out of scope: griddy does not intend to cover it. The table points to the tool that does.

The enumeration covers the __all__ lists of the markov, ergodic, mobility, rank, directional, sequence, and util modules. Where a class has attributes or options with a different answer from the class as a whole, they get their own row. The giddy.plotting functions belong to Rose and are grouped with it. giddy.components is an internal helper for LISA_Markov.spillover().

Coverage table

giddy 2.3.9 Category In griddy, or where to go
markov.Markov: transitions, p Implemented markov_dynamics(), transition_matrix(), with classes from classify_dynamics()
markov.Markov: steady_state, mfpt, sojourn_time Implemented steady_state(), first_passage(), sojourn_time()
markov.Markov: communicating, recurrent, and absorbing classes; multiple steady states of a reducible chain Out of scope The markovchain package: communicatingClasses(), recurrentClasses(), absorbingStates(), steadyStates(). griddy’s chain summaries assume one recurrent class, and first_passage() requires an irreducible chain.
markov.Markov(fill_empty_classes = True) Composition griddy leaves rows with no departures as NA. To fill them: P[is.na(P)] <- 0; diag(P)[rowSums(P) == 0] <- 1 (recipe)
markov.Spatial_Markov: T, P, transitions, p; pooled classes (fixed = True); k, m Implemented spatial_markov() with k and lag_k, transition_matrix(x, lag_class = ...), class_intervals(), lag_intervals()
markov.Spatial_Markov: s, f, S, F Composition steady_state() and first_passage() applied to transition_matrix(x, lag_class = ...) for each lag class; the aspatial s and f come from a markov_dynamics() chain (recipe)
markov.Spatial_Markov: Q, LR, dof_hom, ht, summary() Implemented homogeneity_test(), chi2 and likelihood_ratio rows
markov.Spatial_Markov: x2, x2_pvalue, x2_dof Implemented x2 is the same Pearson statistic as Q, the chi2 row of homogeneity_test(). giddy tests x2 against k(k − 1)² degrees of freedom; homogeneity_test() uses the Bickenbach and Bode count, as giddy does for Q.
markov.Spatial_Markov: chi2 (one test per lag class); markov.chi2() Composition A short function on transition_matrix(x, "count", lag_class = ...) and the pooled counts (recipe)
markov.Spatial_Markov(fixed = False), cutoffs, lag_cutoffs, discrete = True Composition Value classes: classify_dynamics(method = "time_quantile") or method = "fixed" with breaks. Lag classes: join any per-unit, per-period regime to the transitions of a markov_dynamics() chain and count by it. Examples: a spatial lag cut at your own breaks or within each period, or the most common neighbouring class from sfdep::find_xj() (recipe).
markov.Spatial_Markov: shtest; permutation inference (permutations, x2_rpvalue, x2_realizations) Out of scope Use homogeneity_test(). giddy’s documentation advises caution with shtest and chi2 and describes the permutation x2 test as experimental.
markov.LISA_Markov: q, transitions, p, steady_state, move_types, geoda_quads Composition Quadrants from sfdep::local_moran() for each period, passed to markov_dynamics(). Move types are the transition column; GeoDa numbering is a relabelling of the factor levels (recipe).
markov.LISA_Markov(permutations > 0): p_values, significant_moves Composition Join the permutation p-values from sfdep::local_moran() at the origin and destination periods to the chain’s transitions
markov.LISA_Markov: chi_2, expected_t Out of scope griddy has no test that own and neighbour moves are independent. To test whether transitions differ by LISA quadrant, condition on the quadrant and use homogeneity_test() (recipe).
markov.LISA_Markov.spillover() Out of scope spdep::subset.nb() and spdep::n.comp.nb() find connected clusters among units with significant sfdep::local_moran() results, which is what it builds on
markov.kullback() Implemented homogeneity_test(), kullback row, which differs on purpose
markov.homogeneity(), markov.Homogeneity_Results Implemented homogeneity_test() on a list of regime count matrices
markov.prais() Composition 1 - diag(transition_matrix(x)); the scalar Prais–Shorrocks index is mobility_index(x, "prais")
markov.sojourn_time() Implemented sojourn_time()
markov.FullRank_Markov Planned Until then, classify_dynamics(method = "time_quantile", k = n) followed by markov_dynamics() gives the same transition counts (recipe)
markov.GeoRank_Markov Planned Until then, markov_dynamics() with the within-period rank as id and the unit as state gives the same transition counts (recipe)
ergodic.steady_state() Implemented steady_state()
ergodic.mfpt(), deprecated ergodic.fmpt() Implemented first_passage(), for irreducible chains
ergodic.var_mfpt_ergodic(), deprecated ergodic.var_fmpt_ergodic() Composition Kemeny and Snell’s variance formula, using first_passage(), steady_state(), and the fundamental matrix (recipe)
mobility.markov_mobility() Implemented mobility_index(): "P", "D", "L2", "B1", "B2" are "prais", "determinant", "eigen", "bartholomew1", "bartholomew2"
rank.Tau Composition stats::cor.test(x, y, method = "kendall") returns the same tau-b. The asymptotic p-values differ slightly.
rank.SpatialTau, rank.Tau_Local, rank.Tau_Local_Neighbor, rank.Tau_Local_Neighborhood, rank.Tau_Regional Planned Spatial and local decompositions of Kendall’s tau, including the local indicators of mobility association (LIMA)
rank.Theta Composition Rank each period with rank(), take each unit’s rank change between adjacent periods, then compute sum(abs(tapply(change, regime, sum))) / sum(abs(change)) for each pair of adjacent periods. Use sample(regime) for permutation inference. rank_mobility() gives tied values the minimum rank rather than the average, so it reproduces Theta only when there are no ties.
directional.Rose, its permute() and plot methods, and the giddy.plotting functions Planned Rose diagrams of directional LISA vectors
sequence.Sequence Out of scope TraMineR: seqdef() and seqdist() with method = "HAM", "OM", or "OMstran"; transition-rate substitution costs come from seqcost(method = "TRATE")
util.fill_empty_diagonals() Composition As for fill_empty_classes above
util.shuffle_matrix() Composition i <- sample(nrow(X)); X[i, i]
util.get_lower() Composition t(X)[upper.tri(X)] returns the lower triangle in giddy’s row-major order

Worked compositions

The examples use the bundled usjoin panel of state per-capita income. The geometry comes from spData::us_states, and its queen contiguity matches the states48.gal weights in giddy’s examples, so results can be compared with giddy directly.

library(griddy)
library(dplyr)
library(sf)
library(sfdep)

data(usjoin)
data(us_states, package = "spData")

states <- us_states |>
  filter(NAME %in% usjoin$name) |>
  arrange(NAME) |>
  select(name = NAME) |>
  mutate(
    nb = st_contiguity(geometry),
    wt = st_weights(nb)
  )

panel <- usjoin |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(rel_income = income / mean(income)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(year, name)

LISA Markov

sfdep::local_moran() returns each unit’s quadrant. Its pysal column uses the same convention as giddy: the standardized value against its spatial lag. Computing quadrants for each period and passing them to markov_dynamics() gives the LISA Markov chain.

set.seed(2001)
lisa_panel <- panel |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(quadrant = local_moran(income, states$nb, states$wt, nsim = 99)$pysal) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(quadrant = factor(
    quadrant,
    levels = c("High-High", "Low-High", "Low-Low", "High-Low")
  ))

lisa <- markov_dynamics(lisa_panel, name, year, quadrant)
transition_matrix(lisa, "count")
##            
##             High-High Low-High Low-Low High-Low
##   High-High      1087       44       4       34
##   Low-High         41      470      36        1
##   Low-Low           5       34    1422       39
##   High-Low         30        1      40      552

The counts match giddy.markov.LISA_Markov on the same data and weights:

giddy_lisa_counts <- matrix(
  c(1087,   44,    4,  34,
      41,  470,   36,   1,
       5,   34, 1422,  39,
      30,    1,   40, 552),
  nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE
)
all.equal(as.vector(transition_matrix(lisa, "count")), as.vector(giddy_lisa_counts))
## [1] TRUE

The result is an ordinary grd_markov object, so the chain summaries apply:

steady_state(lisa)
## High-High  Low-High   Low-Low  High-Low 
## 0.2856150 0.1419023 0.4049367 0.1675460
sojourn_time(lisa)
## High-High  Low-High   Low-Low  High-Low 
## 14.256098  7.025641 19.230769  8.774648

To ask whether income-class transitions differ by LISA quadrant, condition on the quadrant at the start of each transition and test homogeneity across quadrants:

income_chain <- classify_dynamics(lisa_panel, name, year, rel_income, k = 5) |>
  markov_dynamics(name, year, class)

by_quadrant <- income_chain$transitions |>
  left_join(
    lisa_panel |> select(id = name, from_time = year, quadrant),
    by = c("id", "from_time")
  )

quadrant_counts <- lapply(
  split(by_quadrant, by_quadrant$quadrant),
  function(d) table(d$from_state, d$to_state)
)
homogeneity_test(quadrant_counts)
## # A tibble: 3 × 4
##   test             statistic    df  p_value
##   <chr>                <dbl> <int>    <dbl>
## 1 chi2                  156.    23 9.72e-22
## 2 likelihood_ratio      167.    23 8.76e-24
## 3 kullback              167.    23 8.76e-24

Conditioning on any regime

The quadrant example is a general pattern. Join any per-unit, per-period regime to a chain’s transitions, count by regime, and pass the list of count matrices to homogeneity_test(). spatial_markov() uses the same pattern with pooled quantiles of the spatial lag. Applying the pattern to its lag classes reproduces its result:

spatial <- spatial_markov(panel, name, year, rel_income, geometry = states, k = 5)

by_lag <- income_chain$transitions |>
  left_join(
    spatial$lag_panel |> select(id = name, from_time = year, lag_class),
    by = c("id", "from_time")
  )

lag_counts <- lapply(
  split(by_lag, by_lag$lag_class),
  function(d) table(d$from_state, d$to_state)
)
all.equal(homogeneity_test(lag_counts), homogeneity_test(spatial))
## [1] TRUE

To use your own lag breaks, per-period lag quantiles, or a categorical lag, replace lag_class in the join with that regime.

Conditional chain summaries

The conditional steady states and first-passage times (giddy’s S and F) come from applying the chain summaries to each lag class’s matrix:

conditional_steady_state <- sapply(
  spatial$lag_states,
  function(l) steady_state(transition_matrix(spatial, lag_class = l))
)
round(t(conditional_steady_state), 3)
##       Q1    Q2    Q3    Q4    Q5
## Q1 0.435 0.264 0.204 0.068 0.029
## Q2 0.134 0.340 0.252 0.233 0.041
## Q3 0.121 0.211 0.264 0.290 0.114
## Q4 0.078 0.197 0.254 0.225 0.247
## Q5 0.018 0.200 0.190 0.255 0.337
first_passage(transition_matrix(spatial, lag_class = "Q1"))
##           Q1        Q2        Q3       Q4        Q5
## Q1  2.298353 28.956140 46.142857 80.80952 279.42857
## Q2 33.865497  3.794596 22.571429 57.23810 255.85714
## Q3 43.602339  9.736842  4.910857 34.66667 233.28571
## Q4 46.628655 12.763158  6.257143 14.61565 198.61905
## Q5 52.628655 18.763158 12.257143  6.00000  34.10317

Rank Markov chains

Full rank and geographic rank Markov chains are planned. In the meantime, both can be built with existing functions. These reproduce the transition counts of giddy’s FullRank_Markov and GeoRank_Markov on usjoin. In griddy, rank state Q1 is the lowest income; giddy numbers ranks from the highest.

full_rank <- usjoin |>
  classify_dynamics(name, year, income, method = "time_quantile", k = 48) |>
  markov_dynamics(name, year, class)

geo_rank <- usjoin |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(rank = rank(income, ties.method = "first")) |>
  ungroup() |>
  markov_dynamics(rank, year, name)

dim(transition_matrix(full_rank))
## [1] 48 48
dim(transition_matrix(geo_rank))
## [1] 48 48

Smaller recipes

Pearson tests of each lag class’s counts against the pooled probabilities (giddy’s markov.chi2() and Spatial_Markov.chi2). Their sum is the chi2 row of homogeneity_test():

chi2_vs <- function(counts, reference) {
  expected <- rowSums(counts) * prop.table(reference, 1)
  expected[is.na(expected)] <- 0
  sum((counts - expected)^2 / ifelse(expected == 0, 1, expected))
}

pooled <- Reduce(`+`, lag_counts)
per_lag <- vapply(lag_counts, chi2_vs, numeric(1), reference = pooled)
per_lag
##       Q1       Q2       Q3       Q4       Q5 
## 40.55985 55.47520 17.75290 40.03910 46.79668
giddy_per_lag <- c(
  40.5598541260764, 55.4751973848766, 17.7528996233674,
  40.0390961477108, 46.7966803487369
)
all.equal(unname(per_lag), giddy_per_lag)
## [1] TRUE
all.equal(sum(per_lag), homogeneity_test(spatial)$statistic[1])
## [1] TRUE

Variances of first-passage times (Kemeny and Snell), checked against the example in giddy’s var_mfpt_ergodic() documentation:

var_first_passage <- function(P) {
  k <- nrow(P)
  stat <- steady_state(P)
  Z <- solve(diag(k) - P + matrix(stat, k, k, byrow = TRUE))
  M <- first_passage(P)
  ZM <- Z %*% M
  W <- M %*% (2 * diag(diag(Z)) %*% diag(1 / stat) - diag(k)) +
    2 * (ZM - matrix(1, k, k) %*% diag(diag(ZM)))
  W - M * M
}

P <- matrix(c(0.5, 0.25, 0.25, 0.5, 0, 0.5, 0.25, 0.25, 0.5), 3, byrow = TRUE)
var_first_passage(P)
##          [,1] [,2]     [,3]
## [1,] 5.583333   12 6.888889
## [2,] 6.222222   12 6.222222
## [3,] 6.888889   12 5.583333

Per-class Prais mobility (giddy’s markov.prais()), filling rows with no departures, and giddy’s util.get_lower() ordering:

1 - diag(transition_matrix(income_chain))
##         Q1         Q2         Q3         Q4         Q5 
## 0.08538163 0.17345598 0.20572917 0.15143603 0.06217617
P <- matrix(c(0.5, 0.5, 0, NA, NA, NA, 0, 0.2, 0.8), 3, byrow = TRUE)
P[is.na(P)] <- 0
diag(P)[rowSums(P) == 0] <- 1
P
##      [,1] [,2] [,3]
## [1,]  0.5  0.5  0.0
## [2,]  0.0  1.0  0.0
## [3,]  0.0  0.2  0.8
X <- matrix(c(0, 1, 2, 3, 1, 0, 1, 2, 2, 1, 0, 1, 4, 2, 1, 0), 4, byrow = TRUE)
t(X)[upper.tri(X)]
## [1] 1 2 1 4 2 1

Where griddy differs from giddy 2.3.9

There is one intentional difference. In homogeneity_test(), the chi2 and likelihood_ratio rows match giddy’s Spatial_Markov.Q and Spatial_Markov.LR. The kullback row does not match giddy.markov.kullback() in giddy 2.3.9, for two reasons:

  • It uses origin-state (row) margins for the stratum-specific term. giddy 2.3.9 uses terminal-state margins, which pysal/giddy#260 fixes upstream.
  • It uses the Bickenbach and Bode (2003) degrees of freedom instead of r(s − 1)(r − 1), which overstates the degrees of freedom when some transitions are never observed. See pysal/giddy#265.

With origin-state margins the Kullback statistic is algebraically the likelihood-ratio statistic. With the same degrees of freedom, the kullback row therefore equals the likelihood_ratio row. It is kept for comparability with giddy. See the NEWS entry for 0.2.0 and ?homogeneity_test.

References

Bickenbach, F., and Bode, E. (2003). Evaluating the Markov property in studies of economic convergence. International Regional Science Review, 26(3), 363–392.

Kemeny, J. G., and Snell, J. L. (1976). Finite Markov Chains. Springer.

Rey, S. J. (2001). Spatial empirics for economic growth and convergence. Geographical Analysis, 33(3), 195–214. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1538-4632.2001.tb00444.x

Rey, S. J., Kang, W., and Wolf, L. (2016). The properties of tests for spatial effects in discrete Markov chain models of regional income distribution dynamics. Journal of Geographical Systems, 18(4), 377–398. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10109-016-0234-x
